name: Emeka Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We don't sell anything or campaign for any side, and this conversation is confidential. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Emeka, 43, an experienced electrician repairing homes and wiring small business premises. I have a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence; I handle ordinary faults well enough and call our specialist when the controls get beyond me. My partner Jules cooks in a hospital kitchen, our children are seven and fourteen, and we've a mortgage and five months of expenses saved; my pay is typical and there are some similar electrical firms nearby. I use AI daily to draft anonymous job notes and organise a checklist, checking against the actual circuit and the approved reference; I like finding the failed connection, but dislike typing the same plain explanation three times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a tool that saves ten minutes doesn't need to promise a whole new society. We could use the ten minutes to explain the repair properly to a customer. I'd rather share a small real improvement than sell the crew a giant prediction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our two regular wages cover the mortgage and ordinary costs, with five months saved for a problem or quiet spell. I feel secure in the work I'm doing now. The tool helps me write, but the customer still needs the circuit checked and repaired.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my electrical repair shifts and daily checked notes now and through the next year. Starting next week I'd record how long the notes actually took on ten jobs and discuss the result with the team during the paid Friday meeting. I wouldn't buy another subscription or change the family budget just to keep up with the news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a small improvement I can enjoy without asking it to solve everything. I can turn off the phone after the notes are checked. The children don't need their evening turned into another software trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you judge whether the notes actually helped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare actual note time before and after, not the tool's own claim about minutes saved. I'd also check whether the customer understood the final explanation. A quick record that needs three phone calls tomorrow hasn't saved much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you discuss with colleagues at the meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd invite the colleagues who did the same jobs to say where the records still wasted time. I'd ask the team to decide together what any saved minutes should be used for. That's a conversation, not an agreement I can announce for everybody.

say: I'd value **ten useful minutes** without attaching a whole new society to the tool.
I'd use a small saving for **clear customer explanations** rather than sell colleagues a giant prediction.
think: Our regular wages and **five-month reserve** make the mortgage and ordinary costs feel secure.
My current **repair work** remains needed, with AI helping notes rather than checking the physical circuit.
do: Keep **electrical repair shifts** and daily checked notes through the next year.
Measure note time on **ten jobs** and discuss results in the paid Friday team meeting.
feel: **Calm and interested**, able to enjoy a small improvement while leaving family evenings free from software trials.
S0.quote: A quick record that needs three phone calls tomorrow hasn't saved much.
fieldNote: His **secure baseline** rests on two covering wages and five months saved, without borrowing confidence from the tool's marketing.
He separates **measured note savings** from electrical safety and treats a team discussion as unagreed rather than claiming negotiated terms.

steps.text: Keep electrical repairs and checked daily notes while measuring ten jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team thinking work changes the office first, but we should still ask who gets the saved time. I'd bring the workers' association a proposal for paid learning across office and site staff. A tool that writes quicker shouldn't quietly turn the booking clerk's hours into everybody else's target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my own physical repair hours and our household income to hold for the next few years. I'm uneasy about colleagues getting squeezed by the office changes, not expecting an immediate loss of my wage. I have enough room to test the tool carefully instead of agreeing with every confident suggestion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask colleagues what paid learning they needed and take a shared proposal to the association. During the first year I'd learn the firm's approved AI scheduling checker inside normal paid shifts, comparing ten proposed routes with actual travel and site times. I'd bring errors to the paid team meeting rather than use the tool to judge anyone's speed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for the way the change might be shared, and still curious about the practical use. I like solving a small avoidable problem. I don't want enthusiasm to become an excuse for overlooking the person whose hours got cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare on a proposed route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the real distance, access time and the part collection stop with the suggestion. I wouldn't enter customer names into a practice account. A route that forgets the materials counter isn't a faster day for the electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid-learning proposal were refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the paid-learning terms in writing before calling anything won. If the employer said no, I'd keep the trial inside the paid duties already allowed. The association proposal isn't permission to put unpaid study into everybody's evening.

say: I'd ask **who gains time** when office tasks become faster.
I'd seek **paid learning** through the association for office and site staff together.
think: My own **near-term income** looks secure because most repair work remains physical.
I'm uneasy about **colleagues' hours**, while having enough room to test suggestions rather than accept them blindly.
do: Take a **shared paid-learning proposal** to the association after asking colleagues about their needs.
Learn the **scheduling checker** inside normal paid shifts, comparing ten routes with real travel and site times.
feel: **Uneasy and curious**, interested in practical improvements without overlooking colleagues who might lose hours.
S1.quote: A route that forgets the materials counter isn't a faster day for the electrician.
fieldNote: He explicitly distinguishes **his secure wage** from concern over colleagues' office exposure, supporting unease rather than personal income alarm.
The **routing trial** keeps normal paid shifts and privacy limits, and proposed learning terms remain unagreed until written down.

steps.text: Seek paid learning for office and site staff through the association

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the association thinking AGI arrives in 2028, with capable robots around 2031 for physical work. We need to plan for the office staff's earlier change as well as the site work. I'd rather use the gap to test skills than use it to tell everyone electricians are safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My repair hours could shrink once capable robots handle the physical tasks, and Jules's kitchen work could change too. Five months saved buys time to check options, not a lifelong guarantee for either wage. I think I can act before a big loss becomes fixed, but I'd be anxious about the family mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take a six-week evening course on the electrical controls for ventilation fans, paying its 120 fee from our separate study budget while keeping every basic shift and the five-month reserve intact. In 2029 I'd keep my present repair wage and ask the manager to include some real fan-control repair calls within my normal paid rota, with specialist help where the task exceeded my licence or skill. I'd also help the association seek paid transition learning for both office and site staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with an experiment small enough to afford and check. I could find out the course wasn't for me without emptying the mortgage reserve. I don't think a fan-control title creates shelter from AGI or robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know whether you could take a fan-control job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare what I learned with the actual repair tasks the firm had booked. I'd ask our specialist where I still needed help and check the licence requirements before taking responsibility for anything new. Passing six weeks of study isn't a new licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the firm had no suitable repair calls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the existing paid repairs and stop buying further courses until demand was real. I wouldn't count an imagined maintenance wage in the household budget. The association proposal would still matter, because other workers might not be able to pay even that small fee.

say: I'd distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from capable robots reaching physical work around 2031.
I'd use the gap for **tested learning**, without treating electricians as permanently protected or making office staff wait.
think: Both household wages could lose **physical hours later**, including my electrical repairs.
Our **five-month reserve** gives room to act before a big loss becomes fixed, without guaranteeing either income.
do: Pay the **120 course fee** from separate study funds, retaining every basic shift and the five-month reserve.
Keep **paid repairs in 2029**, requesting fan-control calls only within licence limits and with specialist help beyond current skill.
Seek **paid transition learning** through the association for office and site staff.
feel: **Anxious** with an affordable test, while refusing to treat a new task name as protection from later machines.
S2.quote: Passing six weeks of study isn't a new licence.
fieldNote: He retains **current licence limits** and requests specialist help rather than letting short study become unearned independent competence.
Course spending uses **separate funds**, preserving every basic shift and the five-month reserve; repair demand and future wages remain actual checks.

steps.text: Pay 120 for evening fan-controls study separately, retaining every basic shift and five-month reserve
Keep paid repairs, requesting controls calls within licence limits and specialist help beyond current skill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a chance to test a small course against real work before paying for the next one. Thinking AGI arrives in 2031 and capable robots around 2034. We'd still need shared paid-learning terms, because a longer warning doesn't make every household able to fund its own trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our work and household income look secure in the next few years while I test the course alongside paid repairs. I'm uneasy about the later changes, but not expecting an immediate personal wage loss in this picture. I can check whether new tasks suit me before asking the family to support a bigger decision.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the 120 evening fan-controls course now from the separate study budget, retaining every basic shift and the five-month reserve. I'd keep working with the association on shared paid-learning terms. In 2032 I'd continue paid repairs and request fan-control calls only within my licence limits, with specialist help where needed; I'd pay for no further course until actual booked work justified it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with room to try something and change my mind. I could enjoy learning without pretending the first course was the last answer. The extra years matter because a small mistake needn't become an urgent expensive second mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course useful without overstating your competence?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask whether I could explain the control sequence and diagnose the real fault within my permitted work. Then I'd ask the specialist what still needed checking or a different qualification. A course result is useful evidence, not permission to ignore a limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you share the experience with colleagues?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show colleagues the actual tasks I found difficult and ask what support they needed, too. I'd bring that to the association rather than recommend the same course to everybody. The point is paid room to learn, not selling my own small experiment as a universal route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team ten years should let learning become part of a paid working life, not a never-ending household emergency. I'd still ask for shared terms through the association. I don't want people measured by how many evenings they can afford to give away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our own work and living look secure over the next few years, and an affordable chance to improve at the trade looks positive. I'll be 53 when thinking AGI arrives in 2036 and still need earnings when capable robots follow around 2039. I can prepare without claiming I already know the job I'll hold then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the same 120 evening course now from separate study funds, keeping every basic shift and the five-month reserve intact. Each year I'd check both actual wages, our costs and booked repair demand before buying further study, while the association pursued paid learning. During 2037 I'd keep paid repairs and seek controls calls only within licence limits, with specialist help beyond current skill; I'd review if the actual hours weakened earlier.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about my own position, and interested in getting better at the work without racing a short deadline. I can still have an ordinary weekend with the children. I'd like them to see learning as something adults choose, not just something adults fear they have to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your annual household review measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare real paid hours and essential costs, then ask what equipment had actually been ordered. A forecast could prompt a question, but a changed rota would prompt a decision. I wouldn't wait for 2036 if our wages changed before it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop preparation expanding endlessly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the next course as a question until the work justified it and Jules agreed the budget. More warning isn't permission for me to spend more. The household plan should give us choices, not fill every free evening.

I'd ask for **shared terms** rather than measure workers by the unpaid evenings they can afford.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because our physical wages could be squeezed around 2031 before I've tested many alternatives. Agreed paid learning and honest notice about hours would help, with real repair tasks to practise and specialist checks where I need them. I want a useful new skill, not a new label for the same mortgage worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether being keen on AI makes it easy to forget what I don't know about an awkward circuit. It can, if I let a neat explanation flatter me. I'd rather keep asking the specialist than mistake daily tool use for being the best electrician in the room.

headlineQuote: I want a useful new skill, not a new label for the same mortgage worry.
portrait: At **43**, Emeka is an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, typical pay, and five months of household expenses saved.
He and **Jules**, his hospital-cook partner, have two school-age children and a mortgage, with some nearby electrical employers.
He uses **AI daily** for checked notes and planning, while calling a specialist when a fault exceeds his ordinary competence.
His **progressive outlook** supports shared paid learning; limited separately funded study preserves family reserves without pretending short courses change licence limits.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less time to test alternatives before capable robots could squeeze both physical household wages around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Agreed paid learning**, honest hours notice and real repair practice with specialist checks where needed would help.
